abstract: Sleep is essential for health, and forecasting its evolution could clarify its temporal organization and guide intervention timing. We developed a representation-forecasting model using electroencephalography from 5,419 participants. From 30-minute histories, 10-minute forecasts achieved 90.71% four-class accuracy in the 10% of windows with lowest predicted risk and averaged 72.11% overall. Direction-specific encoder feature axes had spectral correlates. Forecast changes under fixed-strength perturbations along these axes can quantify window-specific sensitivity varying with observed transition destination and bout timing. Physiological validation linked greater simulated perturbation sensitivity to stronger observed sleep-state responses following acoustic stimulation and respiratory events. Clinical profiling linked older age and higher apnoea-hypopnoea index to stronger modeled Wake-directed and weaker N3-directed responses. These results demonstrated that sleep-state forecasting could quantify dynamics, prioritize candidate intervention windows, and help interpret post-intervention changes.
